paper_title: Muon Makes the First Mixture-of-Experts Layer Harder to Balance

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Many open mixture-of-experts (MoE) language models train with Muon instead of AdamW. Most balance the load with a bias on each expert's routing score, adjusted after every step. Their recipes disagree on whether Muon should also train the router. In models with 55M and 108M active parameters, we measure how the optimizer changes the span of these biases, the largest minus the smallest in a layer. The span grows when all tokens favor the same experts, so it shows how hard a layer is to balance. At learning rates tuned on shorter runs, Muon raised the span of the first MoE layer at every seed, roughly doubling it on average, while the other layers changed much less. The rise came from Muon on the rest of the network, whichever optimizer trained the router. In those runs, the inputs to the first router shared a direction, and soon after the warmup its busiest expert averaged four to seven times its fair share. Over the first 3,000 steps, subtracting the batch mean from these inputs removed this overload while barely changing the loss. On the smaller model, halving Muon's learning rate removed most of the rise and slightly improved the loss. Moving only the router to AdamW made the loads shift more during the warmup and slightly raised the loss, so at this scale the results favor keeping the router on Muon.

sections.title: 1 Introduction
sections.content: Most of the leading open language models of 2026 are mixture-of-experts (MoE) models [12, 27, 33, 48, 72]. An MoE layer has many feed-forward networks, the experts, and router that sends each token to few of them [18, 29, 56]. Left alone, the router tends to send most tokens to few experts, which then train on more data and attract still more tokens [56]. Earlier models such as GShard and the Switch Transformer countered this with an auxiliary balance loss that penalizes uneven loads [18, 29, 56]. DeepSeek-V3 switched to auxiliary-loss-free balancing [11, 63], and most recent open models have followed, among them DeepSeek-V4, GLM-5.3, and MiMo-V2.6 [12, 69, 72], some keeping small balance loss as well. Each expert has bias that is added to its score when the router selects experts. After every step, the bias of an expert that received more than its fair share of the tokens moves down by fixed amount, and the bias of an expert that received less moves up. We refer to this balancer as the bias. Most of the leading open MoE models now train their weight matrices with Muon [25, 32] instead of AdamW [35]. Muon orthogonalizes the update of each weight matrix, which sets all the singular values of the update to one. The recipes differ on whether Muon trains the router  (Table 1)  . DeepSeek-V4, Kimi K3, and GLM-5.3 do not exclude it from Muon, while Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, MiMo-V2.6, and IQuest-Q1 do. Only the report of Qwen3.8-Flash-Next gives reasons, among them that Muon made the router unstable early in training with no significant gain later [48]. No report shows data that compare the options, and the studies that compare optimizers in MoE models train without the bias or do not measure the bias itself [28, 32, 36, 37, 59, 61, 64, 70]. The bias pushes the loads toward their fair shares whatever the router prefers, so the loads say little about the router. We measure instead how hard the bias works, by its span, the largest minus the smallest bias in layer (3.2). The span stays near zero when the scores of the router spread the tokens evenly on their own, and it grows with any preference for some experts that all tokens share. When the span is large, the bias decides much of the routing, and the loads stay uneven while it catches up with changes in the scores. We study how the optimizer changes the span in two MoE language models trained on FineWebEdu [45], small one with 55M and large one with 108M active parameters. In each run we choose which optimizer, AdamW or Muon, trains each group of parameters, so that the router, Figure 1: The span, the largest minus the smallest bias of layer, under AdamW and Muon. Left, the mean span of each MoE layer in the main comparison (small model, 1B tokens, seeds 0 to 2), with its range over the seeds. Center, the span of the first MoE layer and the mean span of the other six layers in the same runs, colored as in the left panel, in bins of 100 steps, with the range over the seeds shaded for the first MoE layer. Right, the span averaged over the layers in the tuning runs (0.5B tokens, seed 0) against the peak learning , rate, with filled marks at the rates selected by the tuning. Where marks overlap, at the spans differ by 0.011 or less. The control is Muon without the orthogonalization (4.2). 4 and 3 2.5 10 2 10 3 Muon Makes the First MoE Layer Harder to Balance Introduction the experts, and the other parts of the network can be moved to Muon separately. The backbone is every weight matrix except the routers, the embedding table, and the output head. Runs with the same seed start from the same weights and see the same batches, so within each experiment we compare runs with the same seed, at three seeds. The code and the runs are public (Appendix D). At learning rates tuned for each optimizer on shorter runs, Muon raised the span of the first MoE layer at every seed, from 0.084 to 0.194 on average (Figure 1), and it did so again at all nine seeds of three later experiments (4.4). We had expected the opposite. Under Muon the update of an expert has the same size however many tokens the expert receives, which should weaken the feedback in which busy experts become busier. The span of the first MoE layer followed the optimizer of the backbone and changed little with the optimizer of the router (5.2). With the backbone on Muon, the inputs of the router of the first MoE layer shared direction, with mean cosine similarity of about 0.4 against 0.07 under AdamW on the small model. At the tuned rates, the mean of these inputs gave every token the same preference among the experts. The bias took hundreds of steps to cancel this preference, and meanwhile, with the bias alone at its usual rate, the busiest expert of the layer received on average four to seven times its fair share. In runs that repeated the first 3,000 steps of both models, subtracting the batch mean from the input of this router removed the overload and changed the loss by less than 0.003 (5.3 and 5.5). None of the settings that put only part of the backbone on Muon reproduced the shared direction, yet two of them raised the span of the first MoE layer more than the whole backbone did, so large span can arise without it (5.3). On the small model, half the tuned rate of Muon trained slightly better at 1B tokens and removed about three quarters of the rise, although the shared direction remained (5.4). bias four times faster halved the rise and removed most of the overload after the warmup, and the rise persisted with an added balance loss and on the large model, where the first MoE layer was still overloaded at the end of training (5.5). With the backbone on Muon, moving the router to AdamW made the loads shift more during the warmup, on both model sizes and at every learning rate of stress test, and at the tuned rates it raised the loss slightly at every seed (5.6). In the large-model experiment, loss spikes occurred only in the runs of Muon with the router on AdamW, although the tuning of the large model had spikes in its run of Muon at twice the selected learning rate. For models of our size, these results favor keeping the router on Muon when the backbone is on Muon, and they point to the first MoE layer as the one most affected by the optimizer. Our models have about 50 to 2,000 times fewer active parameters than those whose recipes motivate the question (6.3). Muon Makes the First MoE Layer Harder to Balance 2 Related Work

GLM-5.3 shares the base model of GLM-5.2 and cites the GLM-5 report, which follows the training setting of GLM-4.5. That setting excludes only the embeddings, the bias vectors, and the normalization gains from Muon [19, 20, 72]. We therefore take the routers of DeepSeek-V4, Kimi K3, and GLM-5.3 to be on Muon, although no report states which optimizer trains the router. sections.title: 5.5 Other Balancers and the Large Model
sections.content: The fast bias halved the rise, from 0.075 to 0.040  (Table 5)  , and cut the excess early overload from 2.84 to 0.54, but the span stayed higher under Muon at every seed. Under either optimizer, the fast bias changed the input cosine and the loss by less than 0.01 on average. In the probe of the ablation, the fast bias left the length of the mean input almost unchanged, and the spread of the rows of the router along it was 0.69 to 1.57 times that of the run of AdamW at seed 3 (Appendix C.3). With the balance loss added to the bias, the span stayed higher than under AdamW at every seed, by 0.081 under Muon and 0.055 with the router on AdamW, and the input cosine by 0.34 and 0.33. For softmax router trained only to balance its loads, with small logits, Wang et al. [65, Prop. 2] show that simplified balance loss, the squared distance of the batch-mean softmax output from uniform, makes shared direction add the same logit to every expert, and they expect this only in part when the loss is auxiliary. In our terms, balance loss should lower the score offset. Our balance loss lowered the score offset of all three recipe partitions and the early overload of both Muon partitions at every seed, as this predicts. Its effects on the input cosine and the common share varied in sign over the seeds. We had predicted that it would also lower the span under Muon, and it did at two of the three seeds (Appendix B). With the router on AdamW, the balance loss lowered this span at every seed, by 0.037 to 0.054. 17 Muon Makes the First MoE Layer Harder to Balance 5 Results Without the bias, Muon kept the usage of the experts more even than AdamW on average over the layers, as Wang et al. [64] found, but less even in the first MoE layer, where the early overload under Muon was 7.7 to 7.9 (Appendix C.3). On the large model, with 3B tokens and its own tuned rates, Muon raised the span of the first MoE layer at every seed, by 0.152 on average, or 112% of the span of AdamW against 108% in the ablation on the small model. The input cosine was 0.61 under Muon and 0.73 with the router on AdamW, against 0.41 and 0.39 on the small model, and the early overload was 6.3 and 7.2, near the ceiling of 8. Nine of the ten planned comparisons of this experiment (Appendix B) held at every seed, and 5.6 gives the exception. The first MoE layer of the large model was still overloaded at the end of training, with its busiest expert at 2.2 to 2.8 times its fair share over the last 10,000 steps under both Muon partitions against 1.07 under AdamW. In the unchanged runs of the probe of the large model at seed 0, the scores of this layer sank toward zero, into the flat part of the sigmoid, under both Muon partitions, and over steps 2,001 to 3,000 the bias made most of the choices of experts. At seeds 0 to 2, centering the input of the first router kept the scores off the flat part and removed the early overload (Appendix C.4).

In the probe of the large model, centering removed the overload under both Muon partitions, and the loss with the router on AdamW stayed 0.005 to 0.007 above that of Muon at step 3,000. 19 Muon Makes the First MoE Layer Harder to Balance 6 Discussion and Limitations

sections.title: 6.1 An Account of the Rise
sections.content: Our results support the following account. With the backbone on Muon, the inputs of the first router share direction, and by Eq. (3) their mean gives every token the same preference among the experts, in proportion to how much the rows of the router differ along it. Each bias moves by per step, so the favored experts are overloaded until the biases catch up. The span followed the score offset across the arms, and in the planned comparisons that crossed the optimizers of the router and the backbone, the span and the shared direction both followed the backbone. In the 3,000-step probes, centering the input of the first router removed the early overload on both model sizes and changed the loss by less than 0.003. 𝑢 Three questions remain open. First, we do not know what spreads the rows of the router along the shared direction. On the small model, half the tuned rate of Muon and the fast bias each lowered this spread and left the length of the mean input almost unchanged, and in both cases the early overload stayed below twice the fair share. This suggests that the rows move apart because the loads are uneven, since row receives gradient only from the tokens routed to its expert, but we did not test this. Second, we do not know how the routed experts alone on Muon gave the largest span of the ablation at an input cosine of 0.146. The control, which gives every expert an update of the same size without the orthogonalization, had higher span than AdamW at every rate above its tuned rate (Appendix C.1), so updates of equal size may matter, and training only the routed experts with the control would test this. Third, and most important, we do not know why, of the partitions we trained, only the whole backbone on Muon raised the input cosine of the first router to about 0.4. With only the attention and the dense FFN on Muon, every weight matrix that computes the input of this router except the embedding table was on Muon, yet the input cosine stayed at 0.054 while the early overload reached 5.07. The shared direction therefore seems to need the routed or the shared experts on Muon, although the experts shape this input only through the gradients they send back. The routed experts alone were not enough, and no partition other than the whole backbone put the shared experts on Muon.

sections.title: 6.2 The Router and the First MoE Layer
sections.content: At our scale, the comparisons favor the router on Muon when the backbone is on Muon, as do the runs of Lau and Su [28] without balancing bias, while Qwen3.8-Flash-Next keeps its router on AdamW because, according to its report, Muon made it unstable early in training. Qwen3.8Flash-Next is far larger, with 125B parameters of which 6B are active, and its own stress test used model with 25B parameters. Its report shows no data on the router and states neither the balancer nor the loads, so we cannot tell whether the early instability it describes is the warmup churn we measure. The released configuration [49] lists balance loss and no bias, so its router may face different balancer than ours. With the backbone on AdamW, moving the router to Muon, which no recipe we cite does, changed the span of the first MoE layer by on average, with signs that varied over the seeds. In the stress test, the largest absolute router logit under Muon at 16 times the tuned rates averaged 98 over the seeds and reached 170 at one seed, 0.005 while that of router on AdamW stayed below 36 (Appendix C.2). Our sigmoid router has no softmax and runs in single precision, and the stress test had too few loss spikes to tell whether such logits harm training, but in softmax router computed in bfloat16 they could cause the roundoff errors that the router z-loss reduces [74]. and the loss by +0.004 20 Muon Makes the First MoE Layer Harder to Balance 6 Discussion and Limitations In our models, which have no capacity limit, the overload of the first MoE layer had no cost that we could measure. The only possible exception is the loss spikes with the backbone on Muon. At the tuned rates they came only on the large model with the router on AdamW, and otherwise only at 2 to 16 times the selected rates, in the tunings and the stress test. At every one of them except spike with the router on AdamW in the stress test, the span of that layer was 0.99 or more, near its ceiling (Appendices C.2 and C.4). When experts sit on separate devices, busy experts slow down training [29], and with capacity limit the tokens beyond it are dropped [18], so four to seven times the fair share for hundreds of steps would cost time or tokens. Our models, like DeepSeekMoE and IQuest-Q1 [10, 23], have dense block before the first MoE layer, and under Muon the MoE layer after it was still the hardest to balance. Centering removed the overload, but we tested it only over 3,000 steps and in one layer, and the batch mean makes the routing of token depend on its batch, so practical version would subtract running mean. The fast bias lowered the overload, but in the probe of the large model, at one seed, the loads of the first MoE layer still shifted about three times as much as under AdamW (Appendix C.4).

sections.title: 6.3 Limitations
sections.content: Our models have 55M and 108M active parameters, about 50 to 2,000 times fewer than the models whose recipes motivate our question, and they train on at most 3B tokens, about four orders of magnitude fewer. In trained Moonlight and DeepSeek-V2-Lite, which have almost the same architecture but differ in optimizer, balancer, router scoring function, tokenizer, and training data, the mean pairwise cosine similarity of the hidden states is higher in Moonlight, trained with Muon, in the lowest 20 of the 26 layers plotted and lower in the last three [65, Fig. 15], so at scale stronger shared direction under Muon may persist mainly in the lower layers. The input cosine and the early overload of the first MoE layer were higher on the large model, which trained on three times as many tokens as the small one, and we cannot say whether the overload of this layer would settle in much longer run. In Nemotron 3 Ultra, trained with AdamW, the busiest expert of the first MoE layer reached about 12 times its fair share as its training grew unstable, so in large models this layer may be hard to balance under either optimizer, at least in unstable runs (2). We train one architecture on one dataset, with 32 routed experts of which sigmoid router selects 4, shared expert, one dense block before the first MoE layer, and no capacity limit. The experts of the large model are narrower than its width, 512 against 768, while those of the small model are wider, 768 against 512, so the two sizes differ in more than scale. The sigmoid bounds the scores and gives the span its ceiling, which the span of the first MoE layer nearly reached at some steps on both models, whereas the scores of DeepSeek-V4 have no upper bound [12]. We test one balancer, the bias, at two update rates, and add balance loss at one weight. We use one batch size, 65,536 tokens, which sets the noise in the loads that the bias reacts to, and one warmup of 500 steps, inside which the shared direction appeared. We evaluate the models only by their validation loss, which in small models trained on few tokens may not tell routing methods apart [17]. The rates of the small model were tuned with one seed and 0.5B tokens and used with 1B, where half the tuned rate of Muon trained better and removed most of the rise. We did not retune AdamW on the small model at 1B tokens or train the large model with 3B tokens at lower rate of Muon. Bjorck et al. [6] find steeper fall of the best rate with the number of tokens in their models of 50M and 125M parameters than in larger ones, and ours have 55M and 108M active parameters, so the rates of the large model may be above the best for both optimizers. Each comparison of an experiment rests on three seeds, with no correction for the number of comparisons, and several results of the probes rest on one seed. The probes cover only the first 3,000 steps and, like most of the other exploratory analyses, were chosen after seeing the runs. 21 Muon Makes the First MoE Layer Harder to Balance 7 Conclusion

sections.title: 7 Conclusion
sections.content: In MoE language models with 55M and 108M active parameters, balanced by the auxiliary-lossfree bias, Muon raised the span of the first MoE layer to about twice that of AdamW on average, at learning rates tuned on shorter runs. This span rose with Muon on the backbone, whatever optimizer trained the router, and the backbone on Muon gave the inputs of the first router shared direction. On the small model, most of the rise disappeared at half the tuned rate of Muon, which trained better at 1B tokens. Centering the input of the first router removed the early overload in 3,000-step probes and changed the loss by less than 0.003. With the backbone on Muon, moving the router to AdamW shifted the loads more during the warmup and, at the tuned rates, raised the loss slightly. The next questions are whether these effects grow or settle at production scale and whether running mean can replace the batch mean in centering.

sections.title: B Runs and Planned Comparisons
sections.content: Table 9 lists the runs of every experiment. Every one of the 145 runs finished its planned steps. They were trained on rented Vast.ai hosts with four NVIDIA RTX 5090 GPUs each, one run per GPU at time, in 73 hours and 12 minutes of wall-clock time, and the training steps took 252.6 GPU-hours, without counting the setup of the hosts, the evaluation of the specialization on the four domains, and the exploratory runs. Training uses bfloat16 mixed precision with the master weights and the routers in single precision, torch.compile [5] in PyTorch 2.14 [44], and deterministic algorithms, so run trained again with the same seed on the same GPU model reproduces its numbers bit for bit. sections.title: D Reproduction
sections.content: The code, the Python package tfg with its 213 tests, is public at https://github.com/ marcoshernanz/muon-moe-routing, with the commands that train and analyze every run in code/RUNBOOK.md. The tokenized training data are the public Hugging Face dataset marcoshernanz/llm-lab-fineweb-edu-sample10bt-bpe-16384-full, and the directory of every run, with its logs and analysis, is in marcoshernanz/tfg-runs, where claims.csv in the analysis of the main comparison and of the ablation, bias-speed, balance-loss, and large-model experiments lists their planned comparisons with an expected sign, with their outcomes, and some comparisons that the plan set apart. The balance-loss file repeats seven of the planned comparisons of the ablation. The planned comparisons of the stress test and those without an expected sign, with their outcomes, are in Appendix B. The figures of this paper are made from the runs by code/ai-experiments/thesis_figures_2026_09/ extract.py and code/ai-experiments/paper_figures_2026_10/extract.py, and its tables by code/ai-experiments/paper_figures_2026_10/tables.py, which reads the analysis of each experiment from the run dataset.
